newsitem.title: NEPAL: Communists increase gains in Nepal by-elections.
newsitem.headline: Communists increase gains in Nepal by-elections.

text.p: Opposition communists who have won three of Friday's five by-elections have consolidated their position as the largest single party in the Himalayan kingdom's parliament, officials said on Sunday.

"They (the government) have lost the base in the people. Therefore, the Prime Minister should immediately resign," said Madhav Kumar Nepal, General Secretary of the opposition Communist Unified Marxist-Leninist (UML) party.
The UML has won three seats of the five at stake in the parliamentary by-elections, in the process snatching one seat from Prime Minister Sher Bahadur Deuba's Nepali Congress.
Nepalis voted on Friday in the by-elections which were the first popular vote since Deuba's centrist Nepali Congress party formed a fractious coalition government in September 1995.
Officials said counting of votes for one seat was in progress.

Nepal accused his rivals of vote rigging when a re-poll was held in the Rautahat constituency today, but Bhola Kharel, an election official, told Reuters that the complaint had been investigated. "The complaint was baseless," he said.
With its fresh gains, the UML has increased its position from to 90 seats from 87 in the 205-member House of Representatives but still lacks the required majority to force Deuba out.
Deuba's three-party coalition still has a paper-thin majority but the communists said Friday's voting showed that the prime minister had lost the mandate to rule.
"Though we have become the largest party in parliament we do not have the majority to form the alternative government yet," Nepal told Reuters. "But the government should resign."
Analysts see the outcome of Friday's ballots as key to Deuba's political future ahead of his next show of strength with the communists.

The UML is the largest party in the national assembly but the Nepali Congress, which has 86 votes, commands a majority with the help of its partners, the Rashtriya Prajatandra Party, which has 19 members, and the Nepal Sadbhavana Party which has two deputies.
But the RPP is sharply divided over whether to continue with Deuba or join the communists.
Deuba survived a no-confidence vote last month but has promised to call a confidence vote when parliament convenes next month.
Parliamentary elections are not scheduled until 1999 in the kingdom, which ushered in multi-party rule in 1990 under a constitutional monarchy after a bloody pro-democracy movement.
